summary: This document specifies a method to find which Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) server is authoritative for a requested scope, such as domain names, IP addresses, or Autonomous System numbers. It was replaced by RFC 9224.

eli5.summary: There are many registries, and you need to know which one to ask. This describes a directory that points you to the right one. It was replaced by RFC 9224.

questions: how to find the right rdap server
what is the rdap bootstrap service
how does rdap domain longest match work
what format are the iana rdap bootstrap registries
subtitle: How an RDAP client works out which registry server to ask, using JSON bootstrap files published by IANA.

tldr.problem: The RDAP query protocols say how to ask for registration data, but not where to send the query. Domains, IP addresses and AS numbers are each handled by different registries.
tldr.mechanism: IANA publishes JSON bootstrap registries for domain names, IPv4, IPv6 and AS numbers. A client downloads and caches them, finds the longest matching entry for its query, and gets the base URL of the authoritative RDAP server.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7484 has been replaced by RFC 9224, and it was updated by RFC 8521. New work should follow RFC 9224.

today: RFC 7484 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9224, which is now the specification to follow. It was also updated by RFC 8521.

sections.title: The Problem: Where Do I Send the Query?
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) defines how to query and retrieve registration data from registries (RFC 7480, RFC 7482 and RFC 7483). Those documents do not say where to send a query.

This RFC fills that gap. Top-level domains, Autonomous System (AS) numbers and network blocks are delegated by IANA to Internet registries such as TLD registries and Regional Internet Registries. So the bootstrap information that clients need is best generated from data IANA already maintains.

IANA created new registries in a JSON format, called the RDAP Bootstrap Service Registries. A client fetches them, extracts the data, and matches its query against them to find the authoritative server and the right query base URL.
sections.eli5: There are lots of different registries, each in charge of its own list. Before you can ask a question you need to know whose list to look at. This document gives you a directory for that.

sections.title: Structure of the Bootstrap Registries
sections.content:
Each registry is a JSON object with a version (this RFC defines "1.0"), a publication timestamp in Internet date/time format, an optional description, and a services array.

Each element of services is a two-element array: an Entry Array and a Service URL Array. The entries share the same set of base RDAP URLs listed in the second array. Neither array is sorted.

  • Clients SHOULD prefer secure URLs: if both HTTPS and HTTP are listed, try HTTPS first.
  • Base RDAP URLs MUST end with a trailing /, because query segments are appended to them.
  • Unrecognized JSON properties or values MUST be ignored.
  • Internationalized domain labels MUST appear in A-label form, and domain labels MUST be lowercase.
sections.eli5: Each page of the directory lists a group of names, and next to the group is the address of the office that handles all of them. If an office has a back door and a front door, use the safer front door first.

sections.title: Matching a Query to a Server
sections.content:
There are four registries, one per kind of object, and each has its own matching rule.

  • Domain names: a label-wise longest match from right to left. A query for a.b.example.com that matches both com and example.com uses example.com. Matching is per label, so an entry goodexample.com does not match a query for example.com. The root of the name space is the entry "".
  • IPv4 and IPv6: the longest prefix match, done as for routing by comparing the addresses in binary. Entries use CIDR format for IPv4 and the text representation of prefixes for IPv6. A covering prefix can point at one server while more specific prefixes inside it point at another.
  • AS numbers: entries are ranges written like 64512-65534. A single AS number is written as a range of two identical numbers, such as 2045-2045.

Once the entry is found, the client picks one base URL from the Service URL Array and appends the query segment defined in RFC 7482. In the RFC's example, a query for AS 65411 becomes https://example.net/rdaprir2/autnum/65411. If a server does not answer, the client can try another URL from the array.

Entities such as contacts, registrants and registrars cannot be bootstrapped this way, because there is no global name space for them. Section 7 adds that if the requested value is not in the registry, the client SHOULD give the user an appropriate error message.
sections.eli5: To find the right office, you look for the most specific match. If one sign says "all of com" and another says "example.com", the more specific one wins.

sections.title: Caching, Misses and Limits
sections.content:
Clients SHOULD NOT fetch the registry on every RDAP request. They SHOULD cache it and use signaling from the underlying protocol, such as the HTTP Expires header field, to know when to refresh.

If a query matches nothing in the cached copy, the RFC suggests options. For a domain, the client may query the DNS for the TLD's NS records: if the answer is negative there is no need to refetch, but if it is positive the cached registry may be out of date. A client may also use an RDAP aggregator or redirector that it knows and trusts. The RFC warns that a newly allocated TLD, IP range or AS range may not yet have a bootstrap entry, because the RDAP server may go live and be registered later.

The method does not cover entities, nameservers, help, or search patterns that lack a terminating string matching some entries in the registries.
sections.eli5: You should keep a copy of the directory instead of running to the lobby every time. If a name is missing, your copy might just be old, so check again before giving up.

sections.title: Security and the IANA Registries
sections.content:
Bootstrapping helps ensure that users get RDAP data from an authoritative source instead of rogue sources. The method has the same security properties as RDAP itself, and the registries can be fetched over TLS, which IANA supports.

IANA created the four registries (IPv4, IPv6, AS numbers and domain names) under a new top-level group called "Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP)" on its Protocol Registries page. They are generated from IANA's own allocation registries plus the RDAP server information that registrants supply, and they started empty. Because software will download them, the document expects unusually high demand and notes that the content type MUST be application/json.
sections.eli5: The directory is kept by the people who already hand out the names and numbers, so you can trust it. At first it was empty and filled up as offices told them where to find them.
